learningObjective: Explain when a producer-consumer relation between two ops in a tensor IR permits fusion into a single kernel and when it does not.

canonicalClaims.claim: Producer-consumer fusion that avoids materializing the intermediate tensor requires that per-element production by P and per-element consumption by C share (or are tileable into) a common iteration space, so consumed elements are produced on demand at the consumer's iteration site.
conditions: P and C operate over tensor values with a defined per-element production/consumption.
The compiler has an iteration-space or scheduling model.
nonImplications: Does not imply every such fusion is profitable; register/instruction-count budgets matter.
Does not imply reductions never fuse — many reduction patterns (softmax, GEMM epilogue) do fuse.

misconceptions.claim: Fusion requires P and C to be written in the same language.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Language identity is a codegen concern; semantic fusion is a data-dependence question.

misconceptions.claim: Fusion applies only when P and C share the same op name.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Fusion is based on data dependence, not op-name equality.

misconceptions.claim: Fusion requires one op to be pure and the other side-effecting.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Typical fusion prefers both being pure; opposite polarity is not required.

misconceptions.claim: Every producer-consumer pair with shared iteration should always be fused.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Register pressure and generated-code size are real costs; too-aggressive fusion spills and slows down execution.

performanceScenarios: Fusing pointwise chains removes intermediate HBM traffic; this is the dominant win in memory-bound tensor workloads.
